name: Geo-blocking Regulation
evidence_rating: moderate: one quasi-experimental JRC study (traffic proxy) and before/after mystery shopping; no ex-post evidence on prices or sales; full evaluation pending
summary: The Commission forecast that banning unjustified geo-blocking would cut online prices by about 0.6% and raise consumer welfare by 0.8%; prices have not been checked since. Outright blocking of foreign shoppers has fallen and a Commission study found cross-border visits to online shops rose by roughly 9-13%, but most cross-border purchases still fail because sellers may refuse to deliver abroad. EU auditors in 2025 found enforcement weak and uneven.

indicators.objective: The 2016 proposal has no financial-statement indicators; the memorandum promised periodic reviews and monitoring of 'the effects of the rules'. A full evaluation was launched in February 2025 (period to end-2024) and had not been published at the time of review

indicators.indicator: Share of successful cross-border purchase attempts (baseline: 37% in 2015 mystery shopping)
indicators.evidence: 2019 mystery shopping (about 9,000 websites): rerouting/denial of access decreased, registration blocking halved, success rate 'slightly increased'; but when cross-border delivery was requested only 1 in 3 attempts succeeded, as delivery refusals (not banned) affected more than 50% of attempts. ECA (2025): geo-blocking still persists.

indicators.indicator: Net effect on electronics market size about +1.1%, net trade expansion +0.4%
indicators.evidence: JRC event study using website traffic finds cross-border intra-EU e-commerce traffic up 9.2-13% after Dec 2018; no study of actual sales volumes.

indicators.indicator: Prices -0.5% offline and -0.6% online; consumer surplus +0.8%; no price increases in any Member State
indicators.evidence: Not measured ex post. Theory (Bourreau & Manenti 2023) predicts lower prices short-run but possibly lower investment and welfare long-run.

indicators.indicator: Enforcement through existing CPC network; limited extra workload
indicators.evidence: Slow empowerment of national enforcement bodies (2020 review); ECA found penalties ranging from EUR 26 to EUR 5m and unclear jurisdiction.

literature.citation: European Commission (2016), Impact Assessment accompanying the Geo-blocking Regulation proposal (executive summary SWD(2016) 174), SWD(2016) 173
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the Geo-blocking Regulation proposal (executive summary SWD(2016) 174)
literature.headline: Lifting geo-blocking: market size +1.1%, net trade expansion +0.4%, prices -0.5% offline and -0.6% online, consumer surplus +0.8%; baseline 37% success of cross-border purchase attempts (2015)
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected small price falls (about 0.5%) and a 0.8% gain for consumers, starting from a baseline where only 37% of cross-border online purchase attempts succeeded.

literature.citation: European Commission (2020), First short-term review of the Geo-blocking Regulation, COM(2020) 766
literature.title: First short-term review of the Geo-blocking Regulation
literature.method: mystery shopping (about 9,000 websites, 2019) and stakeholder input
literature.headline: Rerouting and access denial decreased versus 2015; registration blocking halved; purchase success slightly up; but only 1 in 3 attempts succeeded when cross-border delivery was requested; about 50% of consumers aware of the rules (Feb 2019); too early to assess all effects; no extension to copyrighted content proposed
literature.summary_plain: The first review found less outright blocking of foreign shoppers, but most cross-border purchases still failed because traders refuse to deliver abroad, which the Regulation allows.

literature.citation: Alaveras, Duch-Brown & Martens (2020), Geo-blocking regulation: an assessment of its impact on the EU Digital Single Market, JRC Digital Economy Working Paper 2020-02 (JRC121480)
literature.title: Geo-blocking regulation: an assessment of its impact on the EU Digital Single Market
literature.method: before/after panel regression on page-view data for about 10,000 e-commerce websites (Feb 2018-Oct 2019)
literature.headline: Regulation increased real cross-border e-commerce activity inside the EU by 9.2-13% depending on specification, and EU consumers' cross-border trade with sites anywhere by 11.2-11.9%
literature.summary_plain: Commission researchers found cross-border visits to online shops in the EU rose by roughly 9-13% after the ban took effect.
literature.quality: quasi-experimental (before/after with country-pair controls); traffic as proxy for sales

literature.citation: Duch-Brown & Martens (2016), The Economic Impact of Removing Geo-blocking Restrictions in the EU Digital Single Market, JRC Digital Economy Working Paper 2016/02
literature.title: The Economic Impact of Removing Geo-blocking Restrictions in the EU Digital Single Market
literature.headline: Both consumers and producers would gain from removing geo-blocking; smaller countries gain comparatively more
literature.summary_plain: A simulation behind the impact assessment found both shoppers and sellers would gain from ending geo-blocking, especially in small countries.

literature.citation: Bourreau & Manenti (2023), Selling cross-border in online markets: The impact of the ban on geoblocking strategies, International Journal of Industrial Organization 86
literature.title: Selling cross-border in online markets: The impact of the ban on geoblocking strategies
literature.headline: Geoblocking softens competition; a ban lowers online and offline prices, but when firms can invest in online demand the ban may reduce investment and welfare
literature.summary_plain: A theory paper finds a geo-blocking ban cuts prices in the short run but could reduce firms' investment in online sales in the long run.

literature.citation: European Court of Auditors (2025), Special report 03/2025: Geo-blocking, ECA special report 03/2025
literature.title: Special report 03/2025: Geo-blocking
literature.headline: Progress made, but unjustified geo-blocking persists; weak and uneven enforcement (penalties from EUR 26 to EUR 5m); low awareness of support; recommends examining extension to audiovisual services
literature.summary_plain: The EU's auditors found the Regulation helped but unjustified geo-blocking persists and enforcement differs sharply between countries.
